tagline: A winding parkway designed to frame the Hudson Highlands and Catskills
intro: The Taconic State Parkway runs from Chatham to Kensico Dam through ridges, woods and farmland, with views west toward the Catskills. Gentler northern curves give way to tighter turns and quick climbs and descents in the Hudson Highlands. Designated a State Scenic Byway in 1992, it was laid out by landscape architect Gilmore Clarke to present the Hudson Highlands, Catskills and Taconic scenery, as NYSDOT explains.

Franklin D. Roosevelt proposed the parkway in 1925 to improve access to state parks. Two park commissions built its early sections; construction stretched across four decades, interrupted by World War II, before the final segment opened in 1963. Overpasses were faced in native stone, and plantings on medians and roadside slopes were planned to blend with the surrounding woods. As the road became a commuter route, Westchester sections were widened and rebuilt. The entire parkway joined the National Register of Historic Places in 2005.

Heading south from Chatham, pass the Catskill overlooks near Philmont and continue through Columbia County’s farms and woods into Dutchess County. Beyond East Fishkill, the road enters the rugged Highlands and crosses Clarence Fahnestock State Park. In Yorktown the carriageways separate to cross New Croton Reservoir, before the wider Westchester road leads toward its finish at Kensico Circle.

moments.title: Catskill overlooks near Philmont
moments.text: Near the Philmont exit, overlook parking areas on both sides of the Taconic face west toward the Catskills. The northern parkway’s open, rolling terrain gave designers room for wider curves and distant mountain views. Clarke and other landscape architects worked closely with engineers, often on site. They placed long views on downgrades and long curves, where the scenery would be less distracting. Closer views mattered too: northern sections were routed to show wooded hillsides and farms. Tree branches overhang sections of the northern road, while planned plantings continue the appearance of the surrounding woodland.
moments.notice: The overlooks face west across the landscape toward the Catskills.

moments.title: Clarence Fahnestock State Park
moments.text: For 5.5 miles, the Taconic crosses Clarence Fahnestock State Park without development visible from the highway. The road passes rocky cliffs and outcrops in heavily wooded terrain, with its carriageways separating between two lakes. The park began with Dr. Ernest Fahnestock’s 1929 land donation in memory of his brother Clarence, who died while treating influenza patients after World War I. Its landscape became part of the parkway’s design: medians here were used to enhance scenery and create recreation opportunities. Signs mark the Taconic’s highest elevation, almost 1,200 feet above sea level.

moments.title: New Croton Reservoir
moments.text: In Yorktown, the Taconic’s two carriageways spread 1,500 feet apart, with houses and neighborhoods between them, before crossing New Croton Reservoir on separate bridges. The northbound AMVETS Memorial Bridge curves to echo the surrounding hills. A later southbound steel truss bridge was built during the East Hudson Parkway Authority’s improvements. Below them lies part of New York City’s water supply system. Completion of the New Croton Dam in 1906 enlarged the earlier impoundment; water flows from this reservoir into the New Croton Aqueduct toward the Bronx. The reservoir collects water from all the reservoirs in the Croton Watershed.

practical: Catskill overlooks near Philmont: The Taconic State Parkway permits passenger vehicles only. (checked 2026-10-11)
